{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01V31XzofujRsjTUyeykmD83","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# AI / agentic layer — detail\n2\t\n3\tLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\n6\ttreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\n7\tright after it, before any external exposure.\n8\t\n9\tAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\n10\thypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\n11\tconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\n12\trarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\n13\tA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n14\t\n15\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n16\t\n17\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n18\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n19\tall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\n20\timpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n21\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n22\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n23\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n24\t- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n25\t- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n26\t  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n27\t  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n28\t  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n29\t  design, not by filtering.\n30\t\n31\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n32\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n33\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n34\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n35\t- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n36\t  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n37\t  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n38\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n39\t\n40\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n41\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n42\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\n43\tchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n44\t- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n45\t  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n46\t\n47\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n48\t\n49\t### 4. Retrieval\n50\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\n51\tembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\n52\tpermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n53\t- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n54\t  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n55\t\n56\t### 5. Model access\n57\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n58\tstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n59\t- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n60\t  at the stated threshold.\n61\t\n62\t### 6. Memory\n63\tWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\n64\tan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n65\t- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n66\t\n67\t### 7. Orchestration\n68\tHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n69\t- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n70\t  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n71\t\n72\t### 8. Routing\n73\tSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n74\t- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n75\t  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n76\t\n77\t### 9. Feedback\n78\tCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\n79\tretrieval tuning, or training data.\n80\t- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n81\t  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n82\t  poisoning path.)\n83\t\n84\t## Notes\n85\t- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n86\t  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n87\t  and eval scores — from day zero.\n88\t- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n89\t  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n90\t  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n91\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"b9a5fc27-be55-484d-b3af-d635a1fd1d5e","uuid":"840e3609-543b-4bc0-8093-2111bbf9fa76","timestamp":"2026-10-02T23:24:47.403Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p140aff59\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\ai-systems.md","content":"# AI / agentic layer — detail\n\nLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\ntreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\nright after it, before any external exposure.\n\nAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\nhypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\nconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\nrarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\nA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\nimpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n  design, not by filtering.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\nchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\nembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\npermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n  at the stated threshold.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n  poisoning path.)\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n","numLines":91,"startLine":1,"totalLines":91}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_e4oe2yj3domgrgy4mrysutt3qffszxly7t6no24kylbzu52wcpma","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Customer-support RAG chatbot over help-center docs\n\nYour request didn't say what the help-center platform is, whether the bot can see customer accounts, or whether every doc is public. This plan assumes: **anonymous customers, public published articles only, answers only, and a handoff to a human as the bot's single action.** §1 lists what changes if any of that is false. Please confirm those first.\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** a chat widget on the help center. It answers customer questions only from published help-center articles, cites its sources, and hands off to a human agent when the docs don't cover the question.\n- **Type:** AI (RAG) plus software. A new service that reads from the existing help center and writes to the existing ticketing system. **Not a small build:** outside users can reach it, and customers type personal data into chats.\n- **Dominant constraint:** correctness (answers must match the docs).\n- **Worst failure:** the bot confidently tells customers something the docs don't say, such as a refund, price, security or legal claim, and the company is held to it (cf. *Moffatt v. Air Canada*, 2024 BCCRT 149). If this happens at scale, nobody notices until the damage is done. V4 guards it, and V2 guards the version caused by injected instructions. The runner-up failure is customer personal data leaking through logs or the model provider, guarded by V5.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | first token p95 ≤ 2 s; full answer p95 ≤ 8 s | ASSUMPTION (usual chat expectations; confirm with product) | V0 records a starting value; load test in Phase 3 |\n| Throughput | peak concurrent conversations | UNKNOWN: web analytics / support ops supply peak help-center sessions; needed by Phase 4 to size the canary and rate limits | Phase 4 |\n| Availability | bot 99.5% monthly; when it fails, it shows search results plus the contact link | ASSUMPTION (the existing support path never depends on the bot) | Phase 3 fault test |\n| Index freshness | a published or unpublished article is reflected in the index within ≤ 15 min | ASSUMPTION (a policy change must not be served stale) | V3 |\n| RPO / RTO | index RPO: none needed (it can be rebuilt from the help center); full re-index RTO ≤ 1 h | ASSUMPTION (corpus < 10k articles) | Phase 2 exit |\n| AI inference cost: caps | per turn ≤ 6k input / 800 output tokens and 1 generation call; per session ≤ 10 turns; global daily spend cap with a kill switch | ASSUMPTION (starting caps, tuned from V0 and Phase 4 data) | Phase 1 exit |\n| AI inference cost: per resolved conversation | ≤ 15% of cost per human-handled ticket | ASSUMPTION ratio. The ticket cost itself is UNKNOWN: support ops or finance supply it in Phase 0 | V6 |\n| Transcript retention | 30 days, access-controlled | ASSUMPTION (privacy confirms) | V5 |\n| Operational complexity | 1 service, 1 ingestion job, 1 managed Postgres; on-call stays in the existing team's rota | ASSUMPTION | Phase 4 |\n\n**Missing inputs, and the order changes they would force:**\n1. **Account-aware answers or actions** (order status, refunds). If yes, you need authentication, per-user authorization and human approval on writes before Phase 2. That is a different plan.\n2. **Permissioned docs** (internal, plan-tier or customer-specific). If yes, access must be enforced at retrieval time, and that becomes a risk gate inside V3.\n3. **Platforms:** which help center and ticketing system (Zendesk, Intercom, Salesforce…). This decides the connector and whether the vendor's own bot is a real \"buy\" option.\n4. **Languages, and EU or regulated users.** These add eval sets per language, data residency, a DPIA, and possibly AI-disclosure duties. Legal confirms which apply; the plan builds the disclosure regardless.\n5. **Baselines from support ops:** ticket volume, cost per ticket, CSAT. V6 cannot pass without them.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Phase 0 deploy | LLM provider account; read token for the help-center API; access to the help-center theme to embed the widget | organizational | deployed |\n| Eval set (V1, V3, V4) | approval to use redacted ticket history and search logs; ~40 h of SME labeling (support ops lead) | organizational | built (Phase 0–2) |\n| Investment in retrieval | V1 (the docs can answer enough contacts) | validation | committed |\n| Retrieval and prompt hardening | V3, V4 | validation | hardened |\n| Handoff tool spec | support ops agreeing the ticket shape; write credential for the ticketing API | decision + organizational | specified (Phase 3) |\n| Any customer traffic | V2, V4, V5; legal approving the disclaimer, AI disclosure and topic deny-list | risk/security + organizational | exposed (Phase 4) |\n| V6 threshold | cost-per-ticket baseline from support ops / finance | organizational | V6 cannot pass |\n| Widening past 25%; an annual provider commitment | V6 | economic | scaled / committed |\n| Fixing doc gaps (Phase 5) | a named content owner for each doc area | organizational | committed |\n\nNo surprising structural or runtime dependencies. The help center is the system of record for content, and it syncs one way into the index.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: customer text sent to a third party or logged can't be un-exposed, and the DPA is contractual | Hosted model under a DPA (no training on inputs, minimal retention, region matching customers). Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request:** an employee on the allow-list asks \"How do I reset my password?\" in the widget on the production help center and gets a streamed answer that links to the password-reset article.\n- **Tiers it crosses:**\n  - The widget, behind a feature flag (e.g. LaunchDarkly or Unleash).\n  - The chat service, with conversation state in memory.\n  - Retrieval over a real index of the real public articles, built by the ingestion job: naive chunks, a pinned embedding model, `index_v1`.\n  - The hosted LLM, through a thin model client. System instructions are kept separate, and user text and retrieved text go in delimited data blocks. Hard caps from §1 apply, plus a 20 s timeout.\n  - The answer streams back to the widget, with citation links checked against the URLs that were actually retrieved.\n- **Day-zero operations:**\n  - **Deploy:** a container through the existing CI/CD pipeline, with infrastructure as code.\n  - **Logging:** one OpenTelemetry trace from widget to LLM. Tokens and cost are recorded as a metric on every request. Logs are classified as customer personal data from day one, so they are redacted and access-controlled.\n  - **Monitoring:** alerts on error rate and on spend.\n  - **Rollback:** redeploy the previous image or turn the flag off; for the index, point the alias back to the previous version.\n- **Who can reach it:** staff on the SSO allow-list only, using synthetic questions only (no real customer data). Customers see nothing.\n- **Exit check V0:** a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier. A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline. An injected failure (provider key revoked) fires an alert, and the user gets the degraded \"search results + contact us\" reply. Starting values for latency, tokens/cost per turn and ingestion time are recorded, measured at near-zero load.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 0 tasks (alongside §4):**\n  - Get the cost-per-ticket, volume and CSAT baselines from support ops.\n  - Agree with support ops on what \"resolved\" means. Proposed: no handoff, and no ticket from the same session or email within 72 h.\n  - Start V5 legal and privacy review (it has lead time).\n  - Start the V1 ticket sampling.\n\n- **Phase 1: Defenses and budgets**\n  - **Unlocks:** safe to add capability and, later, to expose customers.\n  - **Depends on:** V0.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Output renderer: only allow-listed help-center links, no images, no raw HTML. This closes the exfiltration path.\n    2. Tool executor allow-list containing only `create_handoff`. It runs only after a user confirmation tied to that specific handoff, and is enforced in code, not by the model.\n    3. Citation-required output guard, plus the refusal template.\n    4. Input and output filters: jailbreak patterns, abuse, the topic deny-list from legal. PII redaction before anything reaches logs.\n    5. Rate limits per session and per IP, the daily spend cap, and an auto kill switch.\n    6. AI disclosure and disclaimer text, sent to legal.\n    7. Injection suite in CI.\n  - **Rollback:** guard config is versioned; revert it or turn the flag off.\n  - **Exit check:** V2. A runaway loop gets cut off at the cap and emits a metric.\n\n- **Phase 2: Retrieval and eval harness**\n  - **Unlocks:** answer generation can be specified.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 1, V1.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Ingestion allow-list: only articles that are public and published. Drafts and internal articles are excluded at the source.\n    2. Metadata on every chunk: article ID, URL, locale, `updated_at`, product.\n    3. Chunking by heading.\n    4. Hybrid search (BM25 + vector), plus a reranker only if V3 needs one.\n    5. Incremental sync (webhook or 5-minute poll) with deletes propagated, plus a nightly full rebuild into a new index version.\n    6. Versioned eval set built from the V1 sample and search logs, including unanswerable questions.\n    7. Eval runner in CI (e.g. promptfoo or an in-house harness).\n    8. The build-vs-buy comparison from §3.\n  - **Rollback:** switch the index alias back to the previous version.\n  - **Exit check:** V3. A full re-index finishes within the RTO.\n\n- **Phase 3: Model access, generation, memory, orchestration, handoff**\n  - **Unlocks:** ready for the canary.\n  - **Depends on:** V3. The handoff contract signed off.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Provider abstraction with retries and backoff, a circuit breaker, a fallback model, and structured output (`answer`, `cited_chunk_ids`, `answerable`).\n    2. Single-chain orchestration: rewrite the query using history, retrieve, generate or refuse, offer a handoff.\n    3. Conversation state per §3 (R1 line). Nothing persists past the TTL.\n    4. Integration with the ticketing sandbox, then production with internal test tickets.\n    5. A \"release bundle\" ID (prompt + model + index + guard versions) on every trace.\n    6. Load test against the latency budget.\n  - **Rollback:** revert to the previous release bundle. Turning handoff off falls back to a static contact link.\n  - **Exit check:** V4 passes on both the primary and fallback models. Support ops signs off on the handoffs.\n\n- **Phase 4: Customer canary and widening**\n  - **Unlocks:** production value; the scaling decision.\n  - **Depends on:** V2, V4, V5; the throughput input.\n  - **Tasks:** steps of 1% → 5% → 25% of help-center visitors, holding at least 3 days per step. At each step, check:\n    - error rate and p95 latency;\n    - a daily SME audit of 50 sampled conversations for unsupported claims;\n    - thumbs-down rate, handoff rate and spend against the cap.\n\n    Measure V6 at 5–25%, then go to 50% → 100%. Breaching the spend cap or the error SLO triggers automatic rollback to the previous step.\n  - **Rollback:** turn the flag down. The old contact path is always live, so there is no point of no return. Sending customer data to the provider is the irreversible part, and V5 guards it.\n  - **Exit check:** V6 passes before going past 25%. An unsupported claim in the audit stays at or below V4's rate.\n\n- **Phase 5: Feedback loop**\n  - **Unlocks:** continuous improvement without poisoning the system.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 4 at ≥ 25%; content owners named.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Thumbs and comments go into an SME review queue.\n    2. Accepted items become eval cases or doc-fix tickets for content owners. Raw feedback never changes prompts or the index directly.\n    3. Weekly report clustering unanswered intents.\n  - **Rollback:** the eval set and prompts are versioned; revert.\n  - **Exit check:** each change merges only if the next eval run improves its target metric with no V4 regression.\n\n## 6. Deliberately deferred\n1. **Logged-in, account-aware answers and actions** (order status, refunds): needs authentication, per-user authorization and human approval on writes. Pull forward if V1 fails, or if account-specific intents are more than 40% of handoffs in Phase 4.\n2. **Memory across sessions:** pull forward if repeat-contact analysis shows customers re-explaining. It needs its own privacy review.\n3. **Routing to a cheaper model, or a semantic cache:** pull forward if V6 fails or passes only narrowly.\n4. **Other languages:** pull forward when non-English sessions pass about 10% (ASSUMPTION) or a market requires it. Each language needs its own eval set and V3/V4 runs.\n5. **Fine-tuning:** pull forward only if V4 still fails after retrieval and prompt fixes. Training on transcripts is R3 and would need a new privacy gate.\n6. **More sources** (community forum, macros, internal knowledge base): pull forward when Phase 5 traces gaps to content that exists only there. Forum content is untrusted, so V2 has to be re-run with it planted.\n7. **An agent-assist copilot for support staff** on the same retrieval: after Phase 4 reaches 100%.\n8. **Other channels** (email, in-app, voice): after Phase 4 has held stable for 30 days.\n\nThe quickest way to tighten this plan is to answer the five missing inputs in §1.
